documents.title: Academic Integrity (Writing Center)
documents.summary: A short Writing Center page that offers help with plagiarism, citation and ethical AI use. Its one rule-bearing sentence names 'unattributed AI use' as academic misconduct, which implies AI use with attribution is acceptable. It sends students to the Office of Community Standards and Compliance for policy questions.
documents.stance_why: The page does not ban or require AI and does not hand the decision to instructors. It lists 'unattributed AI use' as academic misconduct, so AI use with attribution is implicitly allowed on condition of disclosure; I code permit, with the caveat that the page is thin.

units.why: The sentence lists 'unattributed AI use' among forms of academic misconduct, so it classifies improper AI use as misconduct (P36) and implies attribution is expected. It binds students and concerns misuse.
units.anchor: unattributed AI use, and more
units.policy: Unattributed AI use is a form of academic misconduct.

units.why: The Writing Center says it offers 'a supportive, judgment-free space' to help students with sources and AI tools. This is a student-support service, not a rule on use, and no type covers a support service for students, so it is UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: Our Writing Center consultants provide a supportive, judgment-free space
units.uncovered_note: Writing Center consultations offered to help students understand plagiarism, citation and ethical use of AI tools (student support service).

units.why: Students unsure 'how to use AI tools ethically' are invited to talk to the Writing Center. This matches P10 (ask when unsure), although the person to ask is the Writing Center, not the instructor.
units.anchor: or how to use AI tools ethically—we can be a part of that conversation

units.why: Students are pointed to the Office of Community Standards and Compliance for 'what happens if a violation is reported'. This refers to the integrity process (P36) and not to a rule on use; P10 fits less well because the question is about consequences.
units.anchor: with questions about policies or what happens if a violation is reported
units.policy: Students can contact the Office of Community Standards and Compliance with questions about policies or what happens if a violation is reported.

documents.unit: Center for Faculty Excellence (AI Faculty Learning Community), Teaching and Learning at CSU pressbook
documents.title: Example Policy Statements for AI in Higher Education
documents.summary: A faculty learning community page that says no single AI policy fits all and that instructors, departments and programs decide. It then lists five sample syllabus statements from CSU faculty, ranging from required acknowledgment to open permission with caveats. These are exemplars faculty can adapt, not institutional rules.
documents.stance_why: The page states 'AI policy statements will be determined by individual instructors, departments, and programs' and offers samples to adapt. It sets no rule of its own, so the stance is delegates. The samples are not named tiers, so tiers is empty.

units.why: The page says there is likely no one-size-fits-all policy and that statements 'will be determined by individual instructors, departments, and programs'. That is P04 (each instructor or program sets the rule).
units.anchor: AI policy statements will be determined by individual instructors, departments, and programs.
units.frag_start: The AI FLC participants find that

units.why: Hughes-Lynch sample: 'you are required to acknowledge use of AI in any work you submit'. This is a disclosure rule on students (P24) and allows AI on condition of acknowledgment.
units.anchor: you are required to acknowledge use of AI in any work you submit for class
units.frag_start: Because it can also be abused
units.frag_end: any work you submit for class.

units.why: Same sample: text copied from AI 'must be treated as any other direct quote and properly cited'. This is a citation duty (P24); it also treats AI like any source, but the load-bearing demand is citation.
units.anchor: Text directly copied from AI sites must be treated as any other direct quote

units.why: Same sample: 'Other uses of AI must be clearly described at the end of your assignment.' A second disclosure duty, covering uses other than copied text (P24).
units.anchor: Other uses of AI must be clearly described at the end of your assignment.

units.why: Koc sample: 'Do not rely solely on AI tools to complete assignments' and use AI 'as a supplement rather than a replacement'. The student must stay the main problem-solver (P32); P19 fits less because AI is not banned from contributing.
units.anchor: Do not rely solely on AI tools to complete assignments.
units.policy: Do not rely solely on AI tools to complete assignments; use AI tools as a supplement rather than a replacement for your own work.

units.why: Koc sample: using AI 'to generate or modify content to evade plagiarism detection is unethical and violates academic integrity'. This classifies one AI misuse as an integrity violation (P36).
units.anchor: Using AI to generate or modify content to evade plagiarism detection is unethical

units.why: Koc sample: 'Do not assume that AI responses are always correct' because AI 'can generate fake results'. This is a verify-the-output rule (P31).
units.anchor: Do not assume that AI responses are always correct.

units.why: Liu sample: 'Use of AI tools, including ChatGPT, is permitted in this course.' A default-permit rule (P02).
units.anchor: Use of AI tools, including ChatGPT, is permitted in this course.

units.why: Liu sample: students 'are only encouraged to use AI tools to help brainstorm assignments or projects or to revise existing work'. The main use named is brainstorming (P15); revising existing work is a writing use that I fold into this unit.
units.anchor: encouraged to use AI tools to help brainstorm assignments or projects
units.policy: Students are encouraged to use AI tools to help brainstorm assignments or projects or to revise existing work they have written.

units.why: Liu sample: 'It is sorely your responsibility to make all submitted work your own.' Students own what they submit (P29).
units.anchor: It is sorely your responsibility to make all submitted work your own
units.policy: Students are responsible for making all submitted work their own, maintaining academic integrity, and avoiding any type of plagiarism.

units.why: Liu sample warns that AI content 'may not meet the standards of this course, even if you only incorporate such content partially'. It tells students AI output may be poor, which is P31.
units.anchor: the accuracy or quality of AI generated content may not meet the standards

units.why: Liu sample notes AI content 'may not provide appropriate or clear attribution' to original authors while assignments require scholarly sources. This is a caution about AI output quality as a source (P31); P52 does not fit because it is not about licensing.
units.anchor: AI generated content may not provide appropriate or clear attribution

units.why: Liu sample: 'I reserve the right to use various plagiarism checking tools ... including those screening for AI-generated content, and impose consequences accordingly.' The instructor will use detection tools to find misuse (P40).
units.anchor: I reserve the right to use various plagiarism checking tools in evaluating your work
units.policy: The instructor reserves the right to use various plagiarism checking tools in evaluating work, including those screening for AI-generated content, and to impose consequences accordingly.

units.why: Rauschert sample: 'If you are ever unsure about whether collaboration with others, including using artificial intelligence, is allowed or not, please ask me right away.' This is P10.
units.anchor: please ask me right away
units.policy: If you are unsure whether collaboration with others, including using artificial intelligence, is allowed, ask the instructor right away.

units.why: Rauschert sample lets students discuss labs in groups 'and try using AI'. AI is treated like a collaborator under collaboration rules (P45), and AI use is allowed here.
units.anchor: you may discuss them in groups (and try using AI)

units.why: Rauschert sample: 'you must all create your own code, output and answers' for labs. Students may not have AI (or others) produce what they submit, so P19.
units.anchor: you must all create your own code, output and answers

units.why: Rauschert sample: 'Quizzes will be done in class and must be solely your own work.' This rules out outside help, including AI, on quizzes (P22).
units.anchor: Quizzes will be done in class and must be solely your own work.

units.why: Rauschert sample: 'You alone are always responsible for the correctness of the final answers and assignments you submit.' Students own what they submit (P29).
units.anchor: You alone are always responsible for the correctness of the final answers

units.why: Rose sample: AI tools 'like ChatGPT and other copilots are not prohibited in the course.' A default-permit rule (P02).
units.anchor: Artificial Intelligence tools like ChatGPT and other copilots are not prohibited in the course.

units.why: Rose sample: 'we will explore their uses (and potential issues) throughout the semester.' The course teaches AI use as part of the course (P44).
units.anchor: we will explore their uses (and potential issues) throughout the semester

units.why: Rose sample: 'You are required to submit original work (that is not generated by AI) for all assessments.' Students may not submit AI-generated work (P19).
units.anchor: You are required to submit original work (that is not generated by AI)

units.why: Rose sample: 'citing if you use AI-generated text and how you apply it in your work.' A disclosure duty (P24).
units.anchor: citing if you use AI-generated text and how you apply it in your work

units.why: Rose sample: LLMs 'supply inaccurate information and fake citations. Use your information literacy skills to corroborate AI information.' A verify-output rule (P31).
units.anchor: Use your information literacy skills to corroborate AI information

units.why: Rose sample: 'Failure to cite your use of AI or using fabricated information could result in your violation of the Academic Honesty Policy.' Nondisclosure itself is the violation (P28).
units.anchor: Failure to cite your use of AI or using fabricated information could result in

units.why: Schell-Barber sample: use of ChatGPT 'is neither encouraged nor prohibited' on assignments. AI is allowed without a push to use it, so P02 (permit by default).
units.anchor: neither encouraged nor prohibited from use on assignments for GAD 250

units.why: Schell-Barber sample: 'Chat GPT is quickly becoming a communication tool in most business settings.' It gives a career reason for allowing AI (P44).
units.anchor: Chat GPT is quickly becoming a communication tool in most business settings.

units.why: Schell-Barber sample: if students use ChatGPT, 'be sure to revise the content for clarity, conciseness, and audience awareness'. A rule specific to AI in prose (P18).
units.anchor: please be sure to revise the content for clarity, conciseness, and audience awareness

units.why: Schell-Barber sample: ChatGPT 'should not be used as a way to produce first and only drafts'. It limits AI generating the submitted text (P19).
units.anchor: should not be used as a way to produce first and only drafts

units.why: Schell-Barber sample warns ChatGPT 'may not develop high-quality work that earns a passing grade'. It tells students AI output may fall short (P31).
units.anchor: Chat GPT may not develop high-quality work that earns a passing grade

units.why: Schell-Barber sample: 'It is your responsibility to review and revise all work before submitting to the instructor.' Students own what they submit (P29).
units.anchor: It is your responsibility to review and revise all work before submitting

notes: No school, computing or course documents were collected. Document 2 is a set of faculty exemplar statements (none from computing), not an institutional rule; sample statements are coded as written but should not be read as university policy.
